title: Damp explosives might have kept World War One from ending in 1915
dek: One night a fortress gate failed to blow because the charges were damp. Austria-Hungary narrowly avoided immediate collapse—and the program argues that this and similar contingencies explain why World War One continued past 1915 until 1918.
why: The largely-forgotten siege of this fortress reveals how the WWI Eastern Front shaped the ethnic divisions and violence patterns that define twentieth-century Eastern Europe.
who: Readers interested in WWI's Eastern Front, the origins of Eastern European ethnic conflict, or the historical roots of Ukrainian geopolitics.

points.h: A fortress's job is buying time, not winning battles
points.body: Przemyśl's real value was not whether it could stop the Russians, but that it cut off rail lines and supply routes, giving the routed, demoralized Austro-Hungarian field army a chance to breathe. After the front collapsed, the fortress positioned the troops close enough—within tens of miles and weeks of respite—to rebuild discipline and morale, preventing total collapse within the first month and a half of war. From the start, the fortress existed to give an entire army a chance to recover.

points.h: Brusilov's actual objective was Berlin, not Przemyśl
points.body: Russian commander Brusilov insisted on assaulting the fortress not for the city itself but for the Galician rail network it controlled. Capturing it would let him command all transport lines across Galicia, push north, and drive into Germany's industrial heartland of Silesia, reaching Berlin. For him, Przemyśl was only a gate to a larger prize. He believed this supposedly obsolete fortress would fall in days.

points.h: Damp explosives saved an entire defensive line
points.body: On the night of October 6, during a major assault, Russian soldiers reached the top of redoubt number 11 through darkness, set up ladders, and prepared guncotton to blast open the gate while containing the Austro-Hungarian garrison inside. But it had rained that night. The explosives were wet. They ignited with a hiss and smoke but did not detonate. One technical failure—that single gate did not open. Both analysts believe that if the explosives had fired that night, the entire line would likely have collapsed, and the war's course might have been completely different.

points.h: An unnecessary withdrawal turned the fortress into a trap
points.body: By November, when the Austro-Hungarian forces made their second ordered withdrawal, the fortress was no longer strategically necessary. It lacked food for a long siege—the garrison should have evacuated with the army, leaving an empty city. But Przemyśl had become a household name through its September stand, and Austria-Hungary could not bear to abandon the prestige it had already invested. They kept the garrison inside to hold on, turning it into the spark that ignited a series of brutal, futile relief offensives.

points.h: A winter bloodbath in the Carpathians has been forgotten
points.body: To rescue the trapped garrison, Austro-Hungarian forces spent the entire winter fighting the Russians in the Carpathian Mountains. Temperatures dropped to minus 20 degrees Celsius, and neither side had prepared for winter warfare. Combined casualties reached between one and a half and two million—on the scale of the Somme or Verdun. Yet because the Eastern Front is marginalized in historical memory, and because this region endured an even worse war after, this bloodbath has been nearly erased.

points.h: When supplies ran out, horses became rations
points.body: As the siege dragged on, food itself became a weapon. The city held about thirty thousand civilians, one hundred and thirty thousand soldiers, and twenty-one thousand horses. One-fifth of the garrison lay in hospital from malnutrition. At first, horses hauled ammunition and supplies. As the siege lengthened, their fodder was diverted to humans, and the horses themselves were slaughtered for meat. By March 1915, when the siege ended, nearly 100 percent of the garrison's horses were dead—a reminder that industrial war consumed not just men.

points.h: The commander chose a suicidal charge to preserve honor
points.body: With ammunition spent and food gone, the garrison could not actually break out. But commander Kusmanek ordered a final assault—not westward toward home but eastward, toward Kiev and Moscow. Terrain-wise the ground was flatter, but more fundamentally, this direction preserved a legend, a sense of honor, over any real chance of escape. The charge collapsed in a single night. The garrison then ordered all redoubts and bridges destroyed and the remaining horses shot.

points.h: After the siege, three nations faced separate forms of ethnic cleansing
points.body: When Russian forces occupied the city, they applied different methods of cleansing to local Poles, Ukrainians, and Jews. Polish nobility were arrested and stripped of power. Russia denied Ukrainians were an independent nation, calling them "little Russians," closed Ukrainian-language schools and papers, and arrested intellectuals. About one hundred thousand Jews were forcibly expelled; seventeen thousand received notices to leave in late April 1915. Scholars emphasize that this large-scale forced migration of Jews predates Hitler's genocide.
